lead: Public-key cryptography lets two strangers communicate securely without first sharing a secret key. It replaces the shared key with a pair: a public key anyone may see and a private key kept secret. The system rests on one mathematical idea, a trapdoor one-way function. Computing the function forward is cheap; reversing it is practically impossible unless you hold the trapdoor. This pattern carries session keys in HTTPS, signs software updates, and protects UPI transactions. The arithmetic differs across schemes, but the logic is the same.
prereq: You need modular arithmetic, exponents and Euler's theorem from Unit 2, plus symmetric ciphers and session keys from Unit 3; the RSA arithmetic itself waits in 4.2.

blocks.text: A one-way function is a function f from a domain X to a range Y with two properties. First, for any x in X, f(x) is easy to compute. Second, given a random y in Y, finding any x with f(x) = y is infeasible. Easy means a normal computer can do it in a reasonable time. Infeasible means no known method does it in practice, not that no method exists forever. The function itself is public; its hardness is the protection.
f: X → Y is one-way if f(x) is easy for all x ∈ X, but finding x from y = f(x) is infeasible.
blocks.where: X is the input set; Y is the output set; x is the input; y is the output; ∈ means 'is in'.

blocks.text: A trapdoor one-way function adds one secret. It is still infeasible to invert f without extra information. With a secret trapdoor t, the inverse f⁻¹(y) becomes easy. The name comes from a physical trapdoor: the door is locked from outside, but the owner has a hidden opening. When f is also a bijection, meaning every y has exactly one x, some syllabi call it a trapdoor permutation.

sections.h3: Five requirements of a public-key system

blocks.text: A public-key cryptosystem must meet five standard requirements.

items: Generating a key pair is cheap.
Encrypting with the public key is cheap.
Decrypting with the private key is cheap.
Deriving the private key from the public key is infeasible.
Either key can be used first for one direction: public key for encryption, private key for decryption; or private key for signing, public key for verification.

blocks.text: The first direction gives confidentiality. Anyone can encrypt to Alice with her public key; only Alice has the private key to decrypt. The second direction gives authentication. If Alice encrypts with her private key, anyone can decrypt with her public key, so the result is not secret; it proves the holder of Alice's private key produced it. Digital signatures use this direction on a hash; see 4.8.

Symmetric ciphers need one shared key per pair. For n users that is n(n−1)/2 keys. Public-key systems need one pair per user, so n pairs. For 12 employees, symmetric needs 12×11/2 = 66 keys; public key needs 12 pairs. Symmetric ciphers are much faster. AES-128 uses a 128-bit key; RSA-2048 uses a 2048-bit modulus. RSA is used for short values such as keys, not for bulk data.

sections.h3: Hybrid encryption and the family of schemes

blocks.text: Public-key operations are slow, so real systems use hybrid encryption. The sender makes a random session key, encrypts it with the receiver's public key, and encrypts the data with a symmetric cipher under that session key. The public key carries the key; AES or another symmetric cipher carries the data. TLS works this way; see Unit 5.

RSA, ElGamal, Rabin and elliptic-curve schemes all fit the same pattern. Each defines its own trapdoor one-way function. RSA hides a message in modular exponentiation; ElGamal hides it in a Diffie–Hellman-style shared value; elliptic-curve schemes use point multiplication. The details are in 4.2, 4.3, 4.4. Some syllabi call this asymmetric key cryptography. Public-key encryption never replaces symmetric ciphers; it distributes and manages keys. Trusting a public key is a separate problem, handled in 4.5.

figure.caption: The public step 9 → 14 is one modular cube; the reverse is infeasible without the factors of 55 and instant with d = 27.

spec.title: Trapdoor one-way function
spec.aria: A message m = 9 goes through public f(x)=x³ mod 55 to 14; reversing without the trapdoor is infeasible, and reversing with d=27 is fast.

examples.question: A firm has 12 employees. (a) How many symmetric keys are needed for every pair to talk privately? (b) How many public-key pairs? (c) For n = 55 and f(x) = x³ mod 55, compute f(9). Given 55 = 5×11, φ(55) = 40 and e = 3, find d with 3d ≡ 1 mod 40 and compute 14^d mod 55.
steps: Symmetric keys for n people = n(n−1)/2 = 12×11/2 = 66 keys.
Public-key system: each person has one pair; 12 public + 12 private = 12 pairs, not 66.
examples.answer: Symmetric keys = 66, public-key pairs = 12, f(9) = 14, φ(55) = 40, d = 27, and 14²⁷ mod 55 = 9.
examples.check:
n = 12
sym = n*(n-1)//2
pairs = n
f9 = pow(9, 3, 55)
phi = (5-1)*(11-1)
d = pow(3, -1, 40)
back = pow(14, d, 55)
print(sym)
print(pairs)
print(f9)
print(phi)
print(d)
print(back)

traps: The public key is not secret. Keeping it secret defeats the purpose; the private key is the secret.
Encrypting with the private key does not give confidentiality. Anyone with the public key can reverse it; it gives authentication, as in a digital signature.
Public-key cryptography does not replace symmetric ciphers. It carries a session key; the symmetric cipher carries the data.
A one-way function has no trapdoor by definition, so it cannot decrypt anything. Only a trapdoor one-way function has a fast inverse with secret information.
Not every trapdoor one-way function is a trapdoor permutation. A permutation must be a bijection, so every output has exactly one input.

quiz.q: State the five standard requirements of a public-key cryptosystem.
quiz.a: Cheap key-pair generation; cheap encryption with the public key; cheap decryption with the private key; infeasible private-key derivation from the public key; either key usable first for one direction.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between a one-way function and a trapdoor one-way function.
quiz.a: Both are easy forward and infeasible to invert without help. A trapdoor one-way function also has a secret trapdoor that makes the inverse easy. A plain one-way function has no such secret.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³ mod 55, compute f(9).
A team has 12 members. How many symmetric keys are needed for every pair? How many public-key pairs?
quiz.a: Symmetric keys = 12×11/2 = 66. Public-key pairs = 12, one per member.

quiz.q: Why does encrypting with a private key not give confidentiality? What does it give?
quiz.a: Anyone can decrypt with the matching public key, so the message is not hidden. It gives authentication: only the private-key holder could produce the value, so it works as a signature.

quiz.q: A student says public-key cryptography can replace AES because it is stronger. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Public-key operations are far slower and are used for short values such as session keys. Bulk data uses a fast symmetric cipher such as AES. Real systems combine both in hybrid encryption.
A trapdoor one-way function that is also a bijection, so every output has exactly one input.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems use RSA-OAEP or ECIES for the public-key step, not raw RSA; search those names. Post-quantum cryptography replaces the trapdoor with lattice or hash-based problems; NIST standardisation is the place to follow. The same pattern appears in key exchange for messaging apps and in hardware security modules that keep private keys. A useful next search is 'KEM' and 'hybrid key exchange'.
